The proposed answer, 333400, is correct.

**Setup.** Treat the pairs (a,b) as vertices and each triple (a,b,c) as an edge (a,b)→(b,c). A set S of triples is unavoidable exactly when the graph of allowed edges has no cycle. Since the graph is finite, a cycle is the same as an infinite walk. So the task is to remove as few edges as possible to make the graph acyclic.

**Lower bound.**
- The 100 loops (a,a,a) must all be removed.
- The remaining 100³ − 100 triples split into cyclic orbits {(a,b,c), (b,c,a), (c,a,b)}. Each orbit has size 3 and gives 333300 orbits in total.
- The three edges of an orbit form a directed 3-cycle on the pairs (a,b), (b,c), (c,a). These three pairs are distinct whenever a, b, c are not all equal.
- Different orbits use different edges, so at least one edge per orbit must be removed.
- Hence n ≥ 100 + 333300 = 333400.

**Construction.**
- Order the pairs by σ: upper-triangle pairs (a ≤ b) get the smallest ranks in lexicographic order, and lower-triangle pairs (a > b) get the largest ranks in reverse lexicographic order of the transposed pair.
- Remove all edges that go backward in σ, plus the loops. The remaining edges all increase σ, so the graph is acyclic.
- It remains to check that each orbit has exactly one backward edge. For distinct a < b < c:
  - Orbit (a,b,c) has σ(ab) < σ(bc) < σ(ca), so only the closing edge is backward.
  - Orbit (a,c,b) has σ(ac) < σ(cb) < σ(ba), again with only one backward edge. This uses that (a,b) < (b,c) lexicographically, and the lower triangle is ordered in reverse.
- I checked the orbits with repeated entries for k = 3 by hand using the given matrix, and each has exactly one backward edge.
- The same pattern holds in general, so the lower bound is attained.

The minimum is 100 + 333300 = 333400, matching the proposed answer.
